questions.q: How many lines are in a standard diamante poem?
questions.a: A diamante poem has seven lines. A wrong answer suggests the student has not memorized the basic structural constraint of the form.

questions.q: What does "Line 3" of a diamante poem require?
questions.a: Line 3 requires three "-ing" words (participles) describing the first subject. A wrong answer shows confusion between adjectives and action-based participle verbs.

questions.q: If your diamante starts with "Badminton" and ends with "Chess," what should the nouns in Line 4 represent?
questions.a: Line 4 should have two nouns related to Badminton and two nouns related to Chess. A wrong answer indicates the student missed the "bridge" purpose of the middle line.

questions.q: Analyze this line: "Running, sweating, winning." Does this fit the requirement for a diamante?
questions.a: Yes, it fits if it is in Line 3 or 5, as it consists of three "-ing" words. A wrong answer suggests the student is struggling to identify the grammatical category of present participles.

questions.q: Is it better to choose two completely unrelated subjects for a diamante, like "Pen" and "Planet"? Why?
questions.a: No, it is better to choose related or contrasting subjects (like "Win" and "Loss") because the diamante structure is designed to show a transformation or relationship between them. A wrong answer shows a lack of understanding regarding the poem's thematic purpose.

questions.q: Create a one-line start for a diamante using the subject "Sports."
questions.a: "Sports." Any other word would be incorrect because Line 1 must be exactly one noun.
